title: Functions & Reusable Script Libraries
summary: Stop copy-pasting the same logging and error-handling code into every script. Build a shared library you source once and use everywhere.

sections.title: Building a shared library with source
sections.body:
## Shared Libraries: Stop Reinventing the Wheel

As a team's bash scripting matures, a common and costly pattern emerges: the same logging code, the same environment variable validation, the same retry logic, the same kubectl health check — copy-pasted into ten different scripts. When a bug is found or a convention changes, every copy must be updated. In practice, some copies always get missed, leading to inconsistent behavior and scripts that silently differ from each other in subtle ways.

The solution is the same as in any programming language: **shared libraries**. In bash, a library is a script that defines functions but does not run any code when sourced. Scripts that need those functions load the library with the `source` command (or its shorter alias `.`) and then call the functions as if they were defined locally. This creates a single source of truth for shared logic.

Building a bash library requires a few disciplines that are different from writing a standalone script. The library should **not** call `set -euo pipefail` — that is the caller's responsibility, and setting it in the library would affect the caller's error handling in unexpected ways. The library should **guard against double-sourcing** (being sourced twice) using an idempotency flag variable. And the library should contain only function definitions and constant assignments — no side-effect code that runs on source.

The `BASH_SOURCE[0]` variable is the key to writing libraries that work regardless of where they are called from. Unlike `$0` (which is the name of the running script), `BASH_SOURCE[0]` is the path of the file currently being executed or sourced — so a library can use it to find its own location and load sibling files using relative paths that always resolve correctly.

Every real DevOps codebase has a `lib/` or `common/` directory full of helper functions. You load them with `source` (or the `.` builtin).

```bash
# lib/common.sh — your reusable library
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Do NOT call set -euo pipefail here — callers set their own options
# The library just defines functions; it doesn't run code on source

LIB_VERSION="1.0.0"

# Guard against double-sourcing (idempotent)
[[ -n "${_COMMON_LOADED:-}" ]] && return 0
_COMMON_LOADED=true

# Example helper
require_env() {
    local var_name="$1"
    if [[ -z "${!var_name:-}" ]]; then
        echo "ERROR: required environment variable $var_name is not set" >&2
        return 1
    fi
}
```

```bash
# myscript.sh — loads the library
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Resolve the script's directory so relative paths work wherever you call it from
SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
source "${SCRIPT_DIR}/lib/common.sh"

# Now use the helpers
require_env AWS_REGION
require_env KUBECONFIG
```

Why `BASH_SOURCE[0]` instead of `$0`? When a script is sourced, `$0` is the parent shell's name. `BASH_SOURCE[0]` is always the current file — making relative paths reliable.

sections.title: A proper logging framework
sections.body:
## Logging: Making Your Scripts Observable

When a bash script runs in CI/CD or is executed by an operator responding to an incident, the output is often the only window into what the script is doing and why it might be failing. Scripts that use `echo` ad hoc — sometimes printing to stdout, sometimes to stderr, sometimes with timestamps and sometimes without — produce logs that are frustrating to read, hard to search, and difficult to integrate with log aggregation systems.

A logging framework standardizes this output. The concept is simple: instead of calling `echo` directly, you call `log_info`, `log_warn`, `log_error`, and `log_debug`. Each function adds a consistent timestamp and log level prefix, routes all output to stderr (keeping stdout clean for actual data), and applies ANSI color codes so that warning and error lines stand out visually in terminal output.

The `LOG_LEVEL` environment variable is what makes the framework operationally useful. By defaulting to `INFO` (level 1), the framework suppresses verbose debug output in normal operation. Setting `LOG_LEVEL=0` before running the script instantly enables full debug output — no code changes needed. This is invaluable when debugging a failing CI job: you can re-run with `LOG_LEVEL=0` and see every decision the script made.

The color coding serves a practical purpose beyond aesthetics. When scanning a wall of log output, your eye immediately jumps to yellow (`WARN`) and red (`ERROR`) lines. This means operators can quickly spot the first sign of trouble without reading every line — a significant advantage during an incident when time matters.

Consistent, coloured, timestamped log output makes debugging much easier.

```bash
# lib/logging.sh

# Log levels: DEBUG=0, INFO=1, WARN=2, ERROR=3
LOG_LEVEL=${LOG_LEVEL:-1}

# ANSI colours
_CLR_RESET="\033[0m"
_CLR_GRAY="\033[90m"
_CLR_CYAN="\033[36m"
_CLR_YELLOW="\033[33m"
_CLR_RED="\033[31m"
_CLR_GREEN="\033[32m"

_log() {
    local level_num="$1"
    local level_name="$2"
    local colour="$3"
    shift 3

    [[ $level_num -lt $LOG_LEVEL ]] && return 0

    local ts
    ts=$(date '+%H:%M:%S')
    echo -e "${_CLR_GRAY}${ts}${_CLR_RESET} ${colour}[${level_name}]${_CLR_RESET} $*" >&2
}

log_debug() { _log 0 "DEBUG" "$_CLR_GRAY"   "$@"; }
log_info()  { _log 1 "INFO"  "$_CLR_CYAN"   "$@"; }
log_warn()  { _log 2 "WARN"  "$_CLR_YELLOW" "$@"; }
log_error() { _log 3 "ERROR" "$_CLR_RED"    "$@"; }
log_ok()    { _log 1 "OK"    "$_CLR_GREEN"  "$@"; }
```

Usage:
```bash
source lib/logging.sh

log_info  "Deploying web-app to namespace default"
log_debug "Using KUBECONFIG=$KUBECONFIG"
log_warn  "Replica count is below minimum recommended (2)"
log_error "Failed to connect to cluster" && exit 1
log_ok    "Deployment rolled out successfully"
```

Control verbosity with the `LOG_LEVEL` environment variable:
```bash
LOG_LEVEL=0 ./deploy.sh   # DEBUG: show everything
LOG_LEVEL=3 ./deploy.sh   # silent except errors
```

sections.title: Layered config: env vars, files, and defaults
sections.body:
## Layered Configuration: Defaults, Files, and Environment Variables

Professional scripts need to be configurable at multiple levels. Hardcoded values make scripts inflexible — you cannot use them in multiple environments without editing them. But requiring every value to be set via environment variable makes them tedious to run locally. The solution is a **layered configuration system** where more specific sources override less specific ones.

The standard layering is: built-in defaults (lowest priority) → `.env` file → environment variables (highest priority). This means the script always works out of the box with sensible defaults, can be customized for a specific environment via a `.env` file that lives alongside it (and is git-ignored), and can be overridden at runtime by setting environment variables — which is how CI/CD systems and Kubernetes secrets managers typically inject configuration.

The critical implementation detail is **precedence**: environment variables that are already set in the shell must not be overwritten by the `.env` file. The `[[ -z "${!key+set}" ]]` check (using indirect expansion to test if the variable is set, not just non-empty) ensures this. This means an operator can override any `.env` value by setting an environment variable before running the script — a clean and predictable behavior.

The `check_required_vars` function represents another important pattern: **fail-fast with a complete error message**. Instead of failing on the first missing variable and leaving the operator to discover missing variables one by one, collect all missing variables and report them all at once. This makes the setup experience much less frustrating.

Real scripts have three config layers: defaults → config file → environment variables. Environment always wins.

```bash
# lib/config.sh

# Load a .env file without 'export' leaking into child processes
load_env_file() {
    local file="${1:-.env}"
    [[ -f "$file" ]] || return 0

    while IFS='=' read -r key value; do
        # Skip comments and empty lines
        [[ $key =~ ^[[:space:]]*# ]] && continue
        [[ -z "$key" ]] && continue

        # Strip quotes
        value="${value%\'}"
        value="${value#\'}"
        value="${value%\"}"
        value="${value#\"}"

        # Only set if not already in environment
        [[ -z "${!key+set}" ]] && export "$key"="$value"
    done < "$file"
}

# Validate required variables and print a clear error listing them all
check_required_vars() {
    local missing=()
    for var in "$@"; do
        [[ -z "${!var:-}" ]] && missing+=("$var")
    done

    if [[ ${#missing[@]} -gt 0 ]]; then
        echo "ERROR: the following required variables are not set:" >&2
        printf '  %s\n' "${missing[@]}" >&2
        return 1
    fi
}
```

Practical usage pattern:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
source "${SCRIPT_DIR}/lib/config.sh"
source "${SCRIPT_DIR}/lib/logging.sh"

# 1. Load defaults
NAMESPACE=${NAMESPACE:-default}
TIMEOUT=${TIMEOUT:-300}
DRY_RUN=${DRY_RUN:-false}

# 2. Load .env file (doesn't overwrite existing env vars)
load_env_file "${SCRIPT_DIR}/.env"

# 3. Environment variables from the shell take precedence (already set above)

# 4. Validate what we need
check_required_vars KUBECONFIG

log_info "Config: namespace=$NAMESPACE timeout=$TIMEOUT dry_run=$DRY_RUN"
```

sections.title: Production-grade argument parsing
sections.body:
## Argument Parsing: The Interface to Your Script

A script's argument interface is its API. Just as a poorly designed API creates confusion and misuse, a script with unclear or inconsistent argument handling creates errors and operator frustration. Production scripts used by a team need a clear, documented, and consistent argument interface — not because of aesthetics, but because people under pressure during an incident need to be able to use them correctly without reading the source.

Bash provides a built-in `getopts` for argument parsing, but it only supports single-character flags (`-n`, `-t`) and becomes unwieldy for complex argument sets. The alternative — a manual `while [[ $# -gt 0 ]]; do case $1 in` loop — supports both short and long flags (`-n`/`--namespace`), handles optional arguments, processes flags in any order, and scales gracefully as you add new options. It is more verbose but significantly more readable and maintainable.

The `usage()` function is not optional courtesy — it is operational documentation embedded in the script itself. When someone runs a script they haven't seen before, `--help` should give them everything they need: the argument syntax, all available options with their defaults, relevant environment variables, and concrete examples. A script whose `--help` output is clear and complete is a script that can be handed to a colleague and used without a Slack message to the author.

Environment variable equivalents (`DRY_RUN=true ./script.sh`) are important for CI/CD compatibility. CI systems set configuration via environment variables, and supporting both `--dry-run` and `DRY_RUN=true` makes your script usable from both interactive terminal sessions and automated pipelines without code changes.

Manual parsing with a `while` loop scales better than `getopts` and supports long flags like `--namespace`.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# ── Defaults ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
NAMESPACE="default"
DRY_RUN=false
VERBOSE=false
TIMEOUT=300
APP_NAME=""

# ── Usage ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
usage() {
    cat <<EOF
Usage: $(basename "$0") [OPTIONS] <app-name>

Options:
  -n, --namespace NS    Kubernetes namespace (default: default)
  -t, --timeout SECS    Timeout in seconds (default: 300)
  -d, --dry-run         Print what would happen, do nothing
  -v, --verbose         Enable debug output
  -h, --help            Show this help

Environment variables:
  KUBECONFIG            Path to kubeconfig (required)
  LOG_LEVEL             0=debug 1=info 2=warn 3=error (default: 1)

Examples:
  $(basename "$0") web-app
  $(basename "$0") --namespace argocd --timeout 600 argocd-server
  DRY_RUN=true $(basename "$0") web-app
EOF
    exit 0
}

# ── Argument parsing ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
while [[ $# -gt 0 ]]; do
    case $1 in
        -n|--namespace)  NAMESPACE="$2";  shift 2 ;;
        -t|--timeout)    TIMEOUT="$2";    shift 2 ;;
        -d|--dry-run)    DRY_RUN=true;    shift   ;;
        -v|--verbose)    VERBOSE=true;    shift   ;;
        -h|--help)       usage            ;;
        --)              shift; break     ;;   # end of options
        -*) echo "Unknown flag: $1"; usage ;;
        *)  APP_NAME="$1"; shift         ;;
    esac
done

# ── Validate ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
[[ -z "$APP_NAME" ]] && { echo "ERROR: app-name is required"; usage; }
$VERBOSE && LOG_LEVEL=0

echo "Running with: app=$APP_NAME ns=$NAMESPACE dry_run=$DRY_RUN timeout=${TIMEOUT}s"
```

Key practices:
- Always include a `usage()` function that prints to stdout and exits 0
- Support both `-n` and `--namespace` forms
- Accept `--` to end option parsing (for commands that take args starting with `-`)
- Set env var equivalents (`DRY_RUN=true ./script.sh`) for CI compatibility

sections.title: Exercise: build devops-lib.sh
sections.body:
## Exercise: Building and Using a Real DevOps Library

This exercise asks you to build something you will actually use — a reusable bash library with the components that appear in nearly every real DevOps script, then a consumer script that demonstrates how the library makes the script cleaner, safer, and easier to extend.

The five library functions cover the most common needs: logging (with color and levels), dependency checking (fail if required tools are missing), and Kubernetes state queries (does a namespace exist, is a deployment healthy, how many restarts has it accumulated). Each of these is simple enough to write inline in a single script, but writing them as library functions means every future script that sources the library gets them for free — and improvements to the library (better error messages, additional checks) automatically apply everywhere.

The `cluster-check.sh` consumer script demonstrates how a library changes the character of the consuming script. Instead of low-level shell mechanics, the script reads like a checklist of high-level operations: require kubectl, check namespaces, check deployments, report results. This is the goal of library-based scripting — the consuming scripts express **what** to do, not **how** to do it.

As you implement the library, test each function individually before writing the consumer script. Use `LOG_LEVEL=0 ./cluster-check.sh` to see debug output and verify the library functions are working as expected. Pay attention to how the `deployment_ready` reference implementation handles edge cases like a deployment that does not exist or has zero replicas — these cases matter in a real cluster where some deployments may not be present in every namespace.

Build a reusable library `devops-lib.sh` with these components, then write a script that uses it to check the health of the sandbox cluster.

**The library should provide:**

```bash
# 1. Logging: log_info, log_warn, log_error, log_ok (with colour + timestamp)
# 2. require_kubectl — exits if kubectl is not in PATH or can't reach cluster
# 3. namespace_exists ns — returns 0 if namespace exists, 1 if not
# 4. deployment_ready name ns — returns 0 if desired==ready replicas
# 5. pod_restarts name ns — echoes total restart count for a deployment's pods
```

**The script `cluster-check.sh` should:**

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
source ./devops-lib.sh

require_kubectl

CHECK_NAMESPACES=(default argocd monitoring learning)
FAILURES=0

for ns in "${CHECK_NAMESPACES[@]}"; do
    if namespace_exists "$ns"; then
        log_info "Namespace $ns exists"
    else
        log_warn "Namespace $ns not found"
    fi
done

# Check specific deployments
for deploy_ns in "web-app:default" "argocd-server:argocd"; do
    deploy="${deploy_ns%%:*}"
    ns="${deploy_ns##*:}"
    if deployment_ready "$deploy" "$ns"; then
        RESTARTS=$(pod_restarts "$deploy" "$ns")
        log_ok "$deploy ($ns) — ready, total restarts: $RESTARTS"
    else
        log_error "$deploy ($ns) — NOT ready"
        FAILURES=$((FAILURES + 1))
    fi
done

[[ $FAILURES -eq 0 ]] && log_ok "All checks passed" || { log_error "$FAILURES checks failed"; exit 1; }
```

**Try it in the terminal:**

```bash
# Create files in /workspace
cd /workspace

# Write devops-lib.sh (implement the 5 components above)
vim devops-lib.sh
# or: nano devops-lib.sh

# Write cluster-check.sh
vim cluster-check.sh
chmod +x cluster-check.sh

# Run it
./cluster-check.sh

# Run with debug output
LOG_LEVEL=0 ./cluster-check.sh
```

**Reference implementation for `deployment_ready`:**

```bash
deployment_ready() {
    local name="$1"
    local ns="${2:-default}"
    local desired ready
    desired=$(kubectl get deploy "$name" -n "$ns" \
        -o jsonpath='{.spec.replicas}' 2>/dev/null || echo 0)
    ready=$(kubectl get deploy "$name" -n "$ns" \
        -o jsonpath='{.status.readyReplicas}' 2>/dev/null || echo 0)
    [[ -n "$desired" && "$desired" -gt 0 && "$desired" == "$ready" ]]
}
```
